### 1. Cache Engineering for Agents (2610.28577)
- what: Proposes letting agents drop selected KV entries from attention and reposition retained keys (RoPE) without re-prefilling, and co-designs an AKV serving engine (extended radix tree, segment-batch attention) on SGLang to make this stateful cache reuse work behind a stateless API.
- read: full (text supplied in message; arXiv 2610.28577)
- key numbers: Tool-response rolling drop (keep latest 12 tool responses) vs. Standard summarization at 96K: average score 53.1 vs 51.0 and cost 7.3 vs 11.2 cents for GPT-OSS-120B; 27.7% average cost reduction across three models and four benchmarks. Serving: 1.18x output throughput and 1.51x P95 latency speedup on 8×A800 with SGLang, 100 SWE-bench tasks, and 80 long-context trajectories replayed.
- code/weights: Code at https://github.com/thu-nics/AKV (stated). Weights not applicable (existing models used). The engine is a modified SGLang v0.5.20 on eight A800-80GB GPUs with Mooncake KV transfer, and the headline numbers depend on it.
- practical: LOW
- why: The gains need a modified serving engine with drop/repos operations on hardware he doesn't run, and hosted APIs expose neither. The accuracy margins are small (1.3–2.1 points on 100-task benchmarks, single-judge GLM-5.2 grading with no agreement check), and cost savings are priced on Groq/MiniMax rates with repos charged at a cache-hit rate. The one transferable point for Muninn is that editing earlier context invalidates the cached prefix, so tool-result pruning should happen at cache boundaries, not mid-history. ### 1. Embodied Turing Machines: Stateful Code for Robot Recursive Self-Improvement (2610.12369)
- what: Proposes Code-Only-as-Policy (COAP), a frozen, model-free robot policy written as code that tracks state explicitly, developed offline by a coding agent (Claude Opus 5.5) in a closed loop on RoboDojo's 42 simulated bimanual tasks.
- read: full (text supplied in the prompt; no URL given for the paper beyond the arXiv id)
- key numbers: 70.24% overall SR on RoboDojo vs 31.38% for the best leaderboard entry (PhysicalRSI, agent+VLA) and 27.96% for the best VLA (Simate-beta). - code/weights: not stated. The paper names the RoboDojo benchmark [7] and says results are simulation-only, but I found no code or library release link in the text.
- practical: LOW
- why: The mechanism needs a RoboDojo simulator, a bimanual robot stack, and a frontier coding agent running a multi-hour offline development loop, none of which he runs; the only transferable part is the idea of frozen, state-tracking code with backtracking, which E-05 says to keep at LOW. The headline also rests on a benchmark with no released library, and the leaderboard comparison is against entries whose numbers come from the leaderboard rather than a controlled rerun. ### 1. Harness^2: Recursive Agent Harnessing for an Open World (2610.14224)
- what: Proposes a recursive harness-optimization loop with a label-free contrastive Propose–Probe–Compose step per task (parallel or sequential), plus a library that updates an "improvement harness" across a task stream, evaluated with frozen GLM-5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash under OpenCode/Codex.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL fetched)
- key numbers: WorkBuddy-Bench Avg +11.5 for GLM-5 under OpenCode after one step (base 64.2 → 75.7); JobBench +4.5 for Gemini (31.5 → 36.0 at k=1); LAB Partial +11.8 for GLM-5 (63.6-ish base to ~75 range, per Table 2). Single-run-per-stream means ±1–5 SD, with the paper's own ablations (w/o library 77.5→74.4, w/o composition 75.9) showing gains of 1.6–3.1 points against SDs of 2–4.
- code/weights: github.com/google-research/harness2 and harness2.github.io stated in the paper. I have not checked whether the repo runs or contains the library and prompts.
- practical: LOW
- why: The method is a multi-agent pipeline run by Claude Opus 4.8 as editor and selector, with 200-turn rollouts per task, and it needs a benchmark-specific container harness (WorkBuddy, JobBench, LAB) that I don't have. Nothing here runs on Muninn's stack, and the editor is a frontier model, so the routing and cost benefit is unclear. The transferable idea is "accumulate reusable harness components and reflection lessons, and only retain lessons backed by behavioral contrasts," which is worth noting for Muninn's skills/memory design but doesn't need this paper to test. The label-free evaluation is weak: the Probe step's own authors say contrasts "limit the reliability of the evidence," and the headline deltas come from three runs per cell.

### 1. Into the Unknown: Benchmarking AI agents on open scientific research problems (2610.19159)
- what: Benchmark of 15 open follow-up directions from DOE-lab scientists' papers; nine frontier agents write follow-up papers, graded by an LLM judge against scientist-written rubrics for integrity, completeness and sufficiency.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL given in the supplied text beyond the paper's own project links, which were not fetched)
- key numbers: 0 of 135 submissions valid under strict grading (G1∩G2∩G3); 114/135 fail integrity; only one submission complete (GPT-6-Astra, 1 of 15). Best node-level pass rate on direction rubric is 83.62% (GPT-6-Astra), with open-weight agents at 44–53%.
- code/weights: stated as "publicly available" in the abstract and project links (code benchmark, trajectories, leaderboard, paper viewer). Exact repository URLs are not legible in the supplied text, so I cannot confirm the links.
- practical: LOW
- why: This is a benchmark and evaluation study, not a method you can adopt, and it needs nine frontier harnesses and a GPT-6-Astra judge, so you cannot run the headline result on your hardware within weeks. The grading is also shaky: the judge's paper-level consistency is 86.5% for GPT-6-Astra and 57.7% for Claude-Opus-5.5 (Table 5), the zero-pass headline rests on strict all-node gates, and the rubrics were written by an AI agent and then edited by the scientists. The one transferable finding is the trajectory audit: lenient self-verification (58/64 trajectories) and insufficient backtracking (34/64) suggest that a completion checker derived from the agent's own plan is unreliable, which is worth a check in your Muninn harness. That is a design lesson, not a result that changes a routing decision.

### 1. Next-Concept Modeling: Fast, Parallel Coarse-to-Fine Text Generation (2610.14162)
- what: Trains a multiscale residual VQ-VAE to turn text into a coarse-to-fine hierarchy of discrete codes, then a ~100M transformer generates each level's codes in parallel, so generation takes K≈8–12 steps instead of per-token or many denoising passes.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL fetched, the supplied text is the paper's own)
- key numbers: LM1B Gen. PPL 93.05 at 12 NFE vs MDLM 115.45 and DUO 97.30 at 128 NFE (Table 8); XSum ROUGE-L 28.0 at 8 NFE vs AURORA-LM 26.6 at 128 NFE (Table 2); Sudoku Hard 86.1% vs FMLM+ 81.3% (single run, no seeds reported for Table 3).
- code/weights: GitHub link stated (https://github.com/HazyResearch/ncm); weights not explicitly stated as released.
- practical: LOW
- why: The mechanism is a from-scratch training recipe (tokenizer plus ~100M generator trained for 50k–350k steps on multi-GPU-scale budgets), and nothing in it runs on Muninn's stack, remex/remax, or browser WebGPU inference; the "coarse-to-fine residual codes" idea is a general principle, not a component he could swap in within weeks. The speedup is mostly NFE and wall-clock on a single H100 against baselines that are themselves not tuned for this setup, and the Sudoku and LM1B margins come from single-run numbers with no spread reported, so I'd treat the headline as unvalidated beyond the authors' setup.

- what: Proposes a serving runtime (forked from SGLang 0.5.1) that hosts one subserver per LLM, with async handoff-resume and a delayed-batching scheduler whose threshold comes from a DTMC throughput model, for token-level routing between a small and a large model.

- what: Converts about 100K anonymized social-platform user behavior histories into 91 question-template tasks (Predictive and Rubric), filters by difficulty, generates SFT trajectories with a 2.4T teacher, and fine-tunes Qwen3.6-35B-A3B.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL was given for the paper itself, the code link is https://github.com/AllSpark-Research/Vela)
- key numbers: VelaBench 51.5 → 63.0 (+11.5) for the base model vs. Vela-35B-A3B; general OOD average 54.2 → 58.2 (+4.0), with GPQA-Diamond +4.6 and IFBench +6.7. Difficulty filtering adds +1.1 on user OOD average (single run, no spread reported). RL initialized from the SFT checkpoint reaches 66.2 vs. 58.5 from base (+7.7).
- code/weights: Repo link given (github.com/AllSpark-Research/Vela); the paper says templates, prompts and training/eval code "will" be released. No weights mentioned. Task data is private platform data, so it cannot be rebuilt from the release.
- practical: LOW
- why: The pipeline depends on a private Chinese social-platform behavior corpus, a 2.4T-A95B teacher for composing, scoring and trajectories, and 35B-scale SFT on 75K examples, none of which fits on his hardware or with his data. The transferable idea is a template-based "predict the hidden future from the visible history" task generator, which he could imitate on his own Strava or Bluesky data, but that is a design idea rather than something this paper validates. The gains are single-run, the judge (Qwen3.8 scorer) has no agreement or calibration check, and the headline comparison uses a model with 11.5 points of in-domain gain on tasks the authors generated themselves, so the in-distribution number is inflated by construction. Dataset-generation effects are also confounded with the scoring model.
